headline_marked: [[Sill brings your Mac window or desktop]] to iPhone and iPad, free and serverless
headline: Sill brings your Mac window or desktop to iPhone and iPad, free and serverless
summary: Sill is a free app that mirrors your Mac's screen or individual windows to your iPhone or iPad, offering full control via touch, trackpad, keyboard, or Apple Pencil, with no accounts or servers involved.
details: Sill allows users to view and control any window from their Mac, or the entire desktop, directly on their iPhone or iPad. It supports interaction via touch, a trackpad, a keyboard, or Apple Pencil, making remote control intuitive.

The application works by capturing the Mac's window, encoding it as HEVC video, and streaming it to the Sill app on the iOS/iPadOS device. User inputs like taps, clicks, scrolls, and key presses are sent back to the Mac in real-time.

Connections can be established over the same local network, via a USB cable, using Direct Wireless Connection when no shared network is available, or through a personal VPN like Tailscale for remote access. Crucially, there are no accounts or intermediary servers involved, ensuring direct peer-to-peer communication.

Sill for Mac is available as a free, notarized download from getsill.app and can also be installed via Homebrew. The Sill app for iPhone and iPad is free on the App Store, with the option to build it from source for developers.

Key limitations include displaying only one window or the whole desktop at a time, and it does not transmit sound from the Mac. The clipboard supports text only, up to 256KB, and only between compatible apps. The Mac must remain awake with Sill open.

For security, only paired iPhones and iPads can connect by default, though this setting can be adjusted. Newer versions of Sill for Mac (0.4.0+) and iOS/iPadOS (0.5+) ensure encrypted connections for local network, USB, and Direct Wireless, a critical update from earlier versions.

headline_marked: [[Woman arrested for blocking delivery robot]] in Philadelphia, citing job displacement
headline: Woman arrested for blocking delivery robot in Philadelphia, citing job displacement
summary: A Philadelphia woman was arrested after repeatedly blocking an Uber delivery robot, stating she was protesting against robots replacing human workers. She claims it's her First Amendment right and plans to continue.
details: A woman was arrested in Center City Philadelphia after allegedly refusing to move from the path of an Uber delivery robot. Police responded to the 1200 block of Filbert Street near Reading Terminal Market following reports of a disturbance.

Carolyn Marvin, the woman arrested, stated she was protesting the use of delivery robots. She believes these robots are replacing human workers, leading her to block their progress whenever she encounters them.

Marvin confirmed she has confronted delivery robots on multiple occasions, including a previous incident in September along Broad Street. These encounters have garnered significant attention on social media.

Witnesses described Marvin's actions, with one recalling her saying, "I have to stop this. They're taking over the world." Marvin maintains her right to publicly demonstrate on a sidewalk to protest against delivery robots.

Despite the arrest, Marvin intends to continue her protests. She hopes this viral incident will encourage broader discussion about delivery robots, artificial intelligence, and their increasing role in daily life.
